species.name: Tecopa pupfish
species.habitat: Outflows of two hot springs at Tecopa.
species.threat_summary: Modifying the springs for bathhouses altered flow and temperature; introduced fish are also considered. This is not evidence of extinction by global warming.
species.pdf_threshold_claim: 26–36 °C and never >40 °C: not adopted; the official report describes temperatures differently.

scenario.title: What evidence is missing before comparing aquatic refuges?
scenario.question: We have air temperature, humidity and rainfall from NASA POWER. What would you do before deciding on the aquatic habitat?

choices.label: Use air temperature as water temperature
Pick the site with the smallest p-value
Ask for water data series and habitat evidence

scenario.feedback: Correct: still needed: water temperature, flow, salinity, oxygen, introduced fish. Air temperature is not a substitute for spring water temperature.
scenario.limitations: Complete species card and evidence exercise; there are not yet three aquatic refuge options or validated water series.

variables.label: Annual rainfall
variables.aggregation: Sum of mm/day × days in month

key_variables.brief_favorable_conditions: Desert springs with a stable thermal gradient (26–36 °C, never > 40 °C), continuous flow and shallow oxygenated pools.
key_variables.why_these_variables: Context only: extreme heat and water balance around the springs. The springs are geothermal and were altered by people; spring temperature and flow are not available.
key_variables.rainfall_caution: Reanalysis rainfall is the least reliable NASA POWER variable. Several sites show large multi-year shifts (e.g. Bramble Cay 2015–2025 about 42 % drier than 1981–2014; Monteverde dry-season rain about 3 times higher in 2009–2025 than in 1981–2008). A change-point test places these shifts in different years (1998–2015), so they do not point to a single data-source switch, but they may still be partly artificial. Rainfall forecasts that extend such shifts are uncertain: show the 80 % range and verify against local rain gauges before presenting them as fact.

survival_card.use_rule: Compare the same indicator, unit, annual aggregation and years. Values describe the historical regional grid cell, not measured physiological tolerances. A difference or an out-of-range value does not establish survival or death.

requirements.value: Hot-spring outflows with water around 43 °C (110 °F); the fish could survive 43 °C or more.
requirements.evidence: The brief's '< 40 °C' limit is wrong: the species lived in hotter water than that.
requirements.proxy_note: Air temperature does not describe geothermal spring water.

requirements.brief_value: Continuous flow and shallow oxygenated pools
requirements.value: Unaltered spring outflows. Channelling them for bathhouses made the water faster and hotter downstream than the fish could stand.
requirements.evidence: Altering the natural outflows, not climate, changed the water conditions that killed off the species.

requirements.requirement: No other pupfish or introduced fish
requirements.value: No Amargosa River pupfish (it hybridised with them) and no introduced fish.
requirements.evidence: Channel changes let a related pupfish move upstream and hybridise; introduced species also contributed.

brief_claims_not_supported: Never > 40 °C: it lived in water around 43 °C.
habitat_evidence.use_rule: Ecological evidence only. Prior review labels do not validate numerical survival limits. Do not compare these prose values or indirect proxies with NASA numbers or use them as hard survival rules.
